entries.title: give a `CPtr` its own DWARF type and its own debug-cache entry
entries.body:
`-g` over a program holding a `CPtr` was broken in both compilers, in two different ways, and nothing could see it because no `-g` case had ever named one. `node tests/run.js --parity` could: it compiles the whole corpus under every flag variation, and it saw four rows of stage1 exiting 70 where stage0 exited 0.

Both compilers look a scalar up in an allow-list — a `BASIC_TYPES` table in `src/codegen/debug.ts`, a `switch` in `self/debug.ts` — and a foreign pointer falls out of both, exactly as it falls out of `isPointerParam` and the escape classifier. Here, though, the caller wants a name back. stage0 wrote the miss out as `!N = undefined`, which `llvm-as` rejects; stage1 exited 70 on `debug: no DWARF basic type for type id 12`.

A `CPtr` is now `!DIDerivedType(tag: DW_TAG_pointer_type, baseType: null, size: 64)` in both: DWARF's `void *`, and what `clang -g` writes for one. The width is the whole of what this compiler knows about an address a C function handed back, so the width is the whole of what it says. Pointer-to-`char`, on the strength of the `i8*` a `CPtr` and a string share, was the tempting answer and is the wrong one — a debugger told `char *` prints a foreign address as text.

The second bug was found while writing the first one's test, and is the more serious of the two. `DebugInfo` interns a type's metadata under the name `typeToString` gives it, and the foreign pointer's name is `CPtr` — so is a declared `class CPtr`'s, which is legal source. One program holding both shared a single cache entry under `-g`, and whichever was described first answered for the other: a pointer `malloc` returned came out as `%struct.CPtr*`, which is a debugger reading a field out of memory this compiler never laid out. The foreign pointer is memoised in a field of its own now — it has one form per module and no parameters, so it needs no key at all, and the one it was borrowing was never safe to borrow.

Without `-g` nothing in this path runs and the IR is byte-for-byte what it was.
metrics: 4 of 18 undeclared `--parity` differences closed; 165 runs over 11 programs, 0 undeclared
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: recover from a refused monomorphisation only where the request is a declaration's
entries.body:
A generic whose field puts its own type argument under a constructor is refused by the WP18 §4 termination rule, and both compilers then emitted a *second* diagnostic that the other did not — stage0 saying `inner` is not a field of `Nest$i32`, which it is, and stage1 advising an annotation that is not the fix. Fourteen of the parity mode's eighteen undeclared differences were that one case under fourteen flag variations.

One mistake now produces one diagnostic, and the same one from both compilers. A refused request that is a **declaration's** is answered with the ancestor instantiation whose type arguments it grew: `Nest<i32[]>` is refused and the field is handed `Nest<i32>`, which is exactly the program the sentence tells the reader to write — "name `T` itself". The class the programmer did write keeps its field and its layout, so nothing downstream has to invent a second mistake to describe a type that is missing.

Where the request is an **expression's**, the refusal keeps its throw, and that line is the correction the first shape of this change needed. `expandingStructAncestor` walks the chain `currentStructInstance` maintains, and that chain is live while a struct's members are collected *and* while one of its methods is checked — so `new Nest<T[]>()` inside a method body reached the recovery too, and substituting there bought nothing while costing a sentence about a mistake nobody made, against a mangled symbol nobody wrote. A field's type is a layout and has to be something; the value of a `new` expression is not, it flows into the statement around it. Both compilers tell the two apart by reading what both already maintained: `collectInstanceMembers` is the one caller that clears `currentInstance` while `currentStructInstance` is set.

"One diagnostic" is per offending annotation rather than per program: a class with two fields both naming `Nest<T[]>` has two to fix and is told about both. The function half is unchanged and is now explained by the same rule rather than one of its own, since a generic function is only ever requested from an expression.

Five cases pin it, all agreeing byte for byte between the two compilers under every flag variation: the original, the body trigger, the recovery, two offending fields, and a three-deep cycle.
metrics: 14 of 18 undeclared parity differences closed; 75 runs over 5 programs, 0 undeclared; npm test 1960 passed, 0 failed, 2 skipped, undegraded
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: check parity on the pull request that touches a corpus program
entries.body:
`node tests/run.js --parity` is the only check that asks whether a program or a
flag is still stage0's, and it ran nightly on `main` and nowhere else. That
fixes "nobody remembered to type the command"; it does not stop a pull request
merging a difference, which is how the `CPtr` internal compiler error under
`-g` reached `main` on a green pull request and sat there for four red nights.

The full corpus cannot go on the push path -- measured on `ubuntu-latest`,
13,260 runs over 884 programs in a 36-minute job -- so the check is bounded by
what the pull request touched. `parity-select` maps the diff onto corpus
programs in seconds with no toolchain and publishes the count; `parity-changed`
is gated once at the job level and does not exist at all when the answer is
none, so "a pull request that touches no corpus program pays nothing" is a job
conclusion rather than a step that skipped. The mapping is ownership, not
substring: a `tests/link/<name>/` program owns its directory and every other
program owns its entry and sidecars, so `add.ts` selects `add` and not
`add_plain`. Sixteen checks pin that rule on every `npm test`, because a
selector asserted only by a doc comment could be replaced with a substring
match and leave the suite green -- the same failure one file over from the one
being fixed. Deletions are reported rather than compared: a program that is
gone has no source to compile, but a gate that answers "nothing was compared"
to a diff that removed three cases is describing its own coverage wrongly.

The nightly's `record` job, which opens an issue on a red or unmeasured run,
had never fired -- every red night ran at a SHA predating it. Proved against a
real run rather than read: it opened #93 with the difference table, and the two
conditions carrying it both hold, `inputs` being null off a `workflow_dispatch`
and job outputs surviving a job that failed.

`tests/diagnostic_coverage.js` read the registry with a pattern keyed on four
literal spaces, and `self/codes.ts` has been two-space indented since the arrow
refactor, so it parsed 0 of 408 codes and printed `coverage 0/0 codes` with exit
0. It reads any indentation now, and an empty registry is a failure rather than
a vacuous pass, because nothing else distinguishes "every code is covered" from
"there are no codes".

Measured: parity: 13320 runs over 888 programs (2644.1 s); 0 undeclared
difference(s), 2682 declared -- exit 0, the first zero since WP19 R1 reopened;
diagnostic coverage 0/0 codes before, 344/408 with 64 unreachable after; the
bounded check adds 5 s when no corpus program is touched and 10 s + 47 s when
one is, both in parallel with the rest of CI; npm test 1976 passed, 0 failed,
2 skipped, undegraded
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: the field-shape program WP15 measures the header hoist on
entries.body:
WP15 §2c measured the array-header hoist at 2.48x on a loop whose source
array is held in a class field — the shape `self/` is written in, and
`knownAtMost` in `self/bounds.ts` verbatim — and that number lived only in
the note. §1 of the same note is the standard it is held to: a number with
no program, no flags and no file is not a measurement. `bench/hoist_field.ts`
is the program, so the figure is re-derivable on the reader's own box.

Three scans do the same arithmetic over the same 8192 doubles and differ
only in where the source array is kept: a parameter, a class field, and a
class field read once into a `const` before the loop. They are timed against
each other in alternating rounds inside one process, the way `bench/substr.ts`
is, so a machine drifting under the run drifts under all three.

The third scan is what makes this an acceptance test rather than a stopwatch.
It is the hoist written by hand in the source, measured in the same process,
so the number the emitter has to reach comes from the reader's machine rather
than from §2c's. Under `opt -O3` the parameter and hoisted loops fold their
two lengths into one trip count — an `llvm.umin.i64` in the preheader — and
vectorise; the field loop keeps two lengths, a second exit and a per-iteration
reload of the array's `data`, and does not. That is the criterion §2c insists
on, and why "no header load left in the loop" is not it: §2c reached that
state by hand and measured the program 5 ms slower.

`tests/self/goldens/checked.txt` moves with it. `bench` is a corpus directory
(`tests/self/corpus.js`), so a new program there is compiled by both compilers
and its `--emit-checked` dump is recorded; the diff is one count line and 90
lines of this program's dump, written by `tests/self/goldens.js --update`.
metrics: 2.38x, field shape against parameter shape, on an 8192-element f64 loop
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: give the warning list a deliberate report order
entries.body:
The `performance` warnings of a compilation now have a report order of their
own — by file, then by position in that file, then by diagnostic code — kept as
the list is built rather than left to the order the analysis happened to find
them in.

`src/diagnostics.ts` used to say they needed no sort, because "the analysis
meets them in module load order and then in source order". That was not even
true of the nine pass-2 warnings: a generic's body is checked when one of its
instantiations is *finished* rather than where the generic is written, so a
warning inside a generic already came out after one written further down the
same file. It stops being true altogether for a warning computed in pass 1,
which is what the struct-padding rule will be — without an order it would print
ahead of every warning in its file.

`--json` prints one object per warning, so this is the order of a
machine-readable stream and part of what that stream promises, which is why it
is its own change rather than a side effect of the warning that needs it.

The insertion is deliberate rather than a call into the existing `sorted()`
merge sort: `self/compile.ts` reads the list directly, so the order has to be an
invariant of the list rather than of one accessor, and the two compilers are
worth more when they read alike. The warning list gets a file-order table of its
own, so recording a warning can never move one error in front of another. The
sort is stable and the code is only the last key, so two warnings of one code at
one position keep the order the analysis produced them in.

`tests/cases/diag_order` pins the position key — its first warning is found
third and reported first — and a second leg holds stage1 to the report stage0
produces, built through the stage1 binary the suite already links for the
stage1-only register. The code key is pinned but not falsifiable: every pair of
today's nine warnings that could share a span is mutually exclusive by
construction, so nothing can currently arrive out of code order. The fixture
says so, and the padding warning is what will close it.

Measured: a no-op on today's corpus — 70 warnings over 60 `self/` modules,
`--json` byte-identical before and after, and identical from either compiler;
worst-case reverse arrival costs 69 ms at 800 warnings and 71 ms at 1600
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: an empty flag set fails the parity comparison
entries.body:
The WP19 parity mode reads each compiler's flags out of its own `--help` and
reports what one set holds and the other does not. Two empty sets hold the
same nothing, so they agreed: "the two compilers document the same flags" and
"neither help text was parsed" printed the same green line, and the flag-set
half runs in every `npm test`.

An empty set from either side is now a difference row of its own, returned
instead of the per-flag rows — with one side empty every flag of the other
reads as "stage1's alone", forty rows none of which names what happened. It is
the guard `tests/diagnostic_coverage.js` grew over the diagnostic registry,
in this file's grammar. The `^ {2}` option-line pattern is untouched on
purpose: widening it to `^\s+` would count every flag a description mentions.

The guard is demonstrated rather than trusted. Every run of the mode first
asks the comparison about a help text that names no option, in each pairing
with one that does, and about two that parse and agree — so neither a guard
that stops firing nor a guard that swallows a real difference can pass
unnoticed. It costs microseconds and runs before a compiler is built.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: one shared diagnostic-registry reader
entries.body:
Three places parse the fragment-and-code table back out of `codes.ts`: the code
generator, which preserves every number it has already handed out;
`tests/diagnostic_coverage.js`, which asks which codes the suite reaches; and the
`codes:` checks in `tests/run.js`, which require both compilers to hold the same
table. Three copies of one regular expression is how two of them drifted apart,
and the generator's copy was still keyed on four literal spaces -- exactly the
indentation level `self/codes.ts` lost when WP22 stage C rewrote its tables as
arrows with concise bodies.

The parse is now one module, `scripts/codes-registry.js`. It recognises a pair by
`^\s+`, so indentation is not part of the contract, and it raises rather than
answering an empty registry. It sits beside the emitter that writes the format --
`rows()` in `gen-diagnostic-codes.mjs`, next door -- because #96 is the two halves
drifting apart: stage C changed what the emitter wrote and no reader followed.
`scripts/` also ships in the npm tarball where `tests/` does not, so the shared
module resolves for every caller and the tarball carries five scripts where it
carried four, with nothing removed and no `files` edit.

The generator is the reader that mattered. `existing()` keeps the promise that a
diagnostic code never moves; if its parse returns empty, the per-band watermark
taken from it is lost and the next generation renumbers the whole registry -- and
a code is a published contract that `--json` tools filter on. `--check` does catch
such a renumbering, because it builds in memory and compares against disk. The
trouble is that the remedy a red `--check` prints is to run the generator, and
that run writes the renumbering out. Reading a moved registry has to fail at the
read.

Nothing about the current tree changes behaviour: `existing()` reads
`src/codes.ts` alone, which is still indented four spaces. What goes away is the
condition under which a reindent silently renumbers.

Two checks in `tests/run.js` pin both halves of the guard rather than trusting
them: the live table reindented to two spaces still reads as its full 408 rules,
and the same table with its indentation stripped raises instead of reading as
empty. Each was demonstrated failing with its half of the reader removed.
metrics: reindenting src/codes.ts to two spaces and regenerating moves 349 of 408 codes before this change and 0 after
tests: tests/run.js `codes: the registry reader is indentation-agnostic`
`codes: a registry the reader cannot parse raises rather than reading as empty`
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: warn when reordering a struct's fields would shrink it
entries.body:
WP15 section 8 specifies ten performance rules. The tenth — wasteful struct
padding — is the last of them to ship, and section 8's hint column is the
specification the message meets: it names the size the struct is, the size the
same fields reach in their best order, and the order that reaches it.

`computeLayout` already walks the fields in declaration order, rounding each to
its alignment. It now carries one more accumulator — the sum of the field widths
— and answers that sum rounded up to the struct's alignment as the packed size,
so there is no second walk over a sorted copy. Every field type in the language
has a size equal to its alignment: one byte for `boolean`, a power of two up to
a pointer's eight for everything else. Laying the fields out widest first
therefore leaves no interior gap at all, which makes that number both reachable
and a lower bound on every order — so a strictly smaller packed size is a proof
that a reordering wins rather than a guess that it might.

It is the first section 8 warning computed in **pass 1**, which is what the
report order added in #99 was for: without it a padding warning would print
ahead of every warning in its file. `tests/cases/diag_order_pass1` is the case
`diag_order` could not be — two padding warnings found before a single body has
been checked, two accumulator warnings found after both of them, and a report
that reads the file top to bottom — and stage1 is held to the same report
through the binary the suite already links.

Two shapes stay silent, because section 8's bar is a rewrite the message can
name and neither of them has one: a class that `implements` an interface, whose
first fields are the interface's own and in its order, and a generic
instantiation, which shares one declaration with every other instantiation of
the same class.

Measured: 11 structs over the 60 modules of `self/`, 8 or 16 bytes each, and
nothing anywhere else in the corpus
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: close the padding item and re-state how §8 warnings are ordered
entries.body:
`docs/wp15-performance.md` still described the tenth `performance` rule as
unshipped and blocked, and gave a reason for the block that was not true even
when it was written. Two changes have landed since: the warning list got a
deliberate report order, and the wasteful-struct-padding rule shipped on top of
it. This brings the document, the master plan, and the comment on both sides of
`DiagnosticSink` back in line with the code.

**§9 item 2's padding bullet** is rewritten as a shipped row: `NL9010`, what the
analysis turned out to be, and what the review taught. The layout floor is one
accumulator on a walk `computeLayout` already made — and because every field
type in the language has a size equal to its alignment, laying the fields out
widest first leaves no interior gap, so the floor is both reachable and a lower
bound over every order. That is what makes a `layoutSize` below the declared
size a proof that the rewrite wins rather than a guess that it might.

The ordering concern the old bullet raised was real, and it was closed first in
a change of its own, because the order of `--json` is a contract. What the old
bullet got wrong was the reason. Every §8 warning did *not* come out of one
source-order walk in pass 2: a generic's body is checked when one of its
instantiations finishes, so the class already owed itself an order before a
pass-1 rule existed. And the sort's own change expected this rule to make the
code key falsifiable, which it did not — replacing both codes in
`compareWarnings` with one constant leaves `diag_order`, `diag_order_pass1` and
`perf_padding` byte-identical, `--json` included. That reading is dated in the
document rather than stated as standing, because nothing in the suite pins it.
What `diag_order_pass1` closes is the other key, the one the sort was written
for.

**§8's rule table** gave the padding row a one-line specification and no mention
of the two shapes that stay silent; it now describes what ships, without quoting
message prose that is allowed to change between releases. A paragraph after the
table states the pass split once, where the class is specified, and points at
`docs/LANGUAGE.md` for the order itself — including the "in the order files are
first warned about" qualifier, which is the only non-obvious part of the key and
the part a restatement loses.

**§9's trailer** said the bounds-check opt-out waits on item 6 and a count of
the surviving checks. Both happened and §2.4 records the answer, so §9 now says
what §2.4 says — and points at it for the count rather than restating a
corpus-derived number in a second place.

**`docs/MASTER_PLAN.md`** item 2 said four of §8's warnings were still waiting on
the analyses that feed them. All ten ship.

**Both `diagnostics.ts` files** claimed nothing in the suite would catch the two
compilers disagreeing about warning order. One thing does — the WP15 block of
`tests/run.js` — and it is a counted skip where there is no C toolchain to link
a stage1 binary with, so the comment now says both halves. Neither file carries
a warning count any more: the old one had gone stale, and a corpus count in a
source comment is a count nothing re-derives.

Both comments are rewritten at their original line count. `--emit-checked`
records every local and callee by line, so a line added to a comment in
`self/diagnostics.ts` rewrites 98 lines of `tests/self/goldens/checked_self.txt`
for no change in meaning; at net zero the golden does not move and the five
stage1 goldens agree untouched.

Measured at c656ee3 over the sixty modules of `self/` that declare no `main`:
11 structs reach NL9010, ten spending 8 bytes a value and `ConstInfo` 16, out of
81 performance warnings; 72 of the 83 struct declarations are already at floor
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: hoist an array's header out of the loop that reads it
entries.body:
An array held in a class field now has its header — the field load, `len` and
`data` — read once in the loop's preheader wherever the whole program proves
nothing the loop reaches can grow the array, with **one length value feeding the
loop condition and the bounds check both**.

That criterion is WP15 §2c's, and it is sharp in a way the obvious one is not.
"No header load left in the loop" is satisfiable while buying nothing: a
preheader load *per use* still leaves two length values, two compares and two
loop exits, and §2c reached exactly that state by hand and measured the program
5 ms slower. What the emitter guarantees is one SSA value in both places, by
construction rather than by hoping GVN merges two loads of one address.

The prerequisite was a fact the fixpoint did not have.
`PointerParamFacts.writesThrough` lumps a `push` in with every other store, so a
function that only writes elements is indistinguishable from one that
reallocates the buffer — and an element write leaves the header alone, which is
the whole of what the §2b alias domains encode. `FunctionFacts.resizesArray`
separates the two and propagates over the call graph like any other property of
a closure. Its second consumer is `bodyMayExtend`, which until now read every
user call in a `for...of` body as growing the array; four functions in the
corpus gain `willreturn` from asking the fixpoint instead.

Four things refuse the hoist, and each is the whole of a proof: a `push` or
`pop` the loop can reach, a store in the loop to a field the path names, a path
rooted at a local the loop declares or at a reassignable one, and a link whose
**declared** type is nullable. That last is a miscompile rather than a missed
optimisation if it is got wrong, and the first version did get it wrong: the
checker records the narrowed type inside `if (h !== null)`, and the preheader is
outside that guard, so resolving the path on the narrowed answer put a null
dereference ahead of a loop whose body never ran.

**It does not reach §2c's acceptance number, and the reason is not the hoist.**
`bench/hoist_field.ts`'s field scan does not move once loop alignment is pinned
(755 ms against 753 ms). What separates it from the parameter shape is a second
bounds check, which is a second loop exit, and that check exists because
`src/checker/bounds.ts` keys its length facts by variable and never by a
property path — so `const xs = h.xs` proves `xs[i]` in range while
`h.xs.length` proves nothing about `h.xs[i]`. §2c's criterion is therefore
necessary but not sufficient: what the fast shapes have is one *compare*, from
the checker's proof rather than from any hoist. That work is now issue #106,
and this hoist is what a property-path holder would be proved against.

Measured: 1.96x on an isolated field scan where LLVM had not already hoisted the
reload (1492 ms -> 761 ms); neutral on bench/hoist_field.ts with loop alignment
pinned (755 ms -> 753 ms); self/bounds.ts 25 -> 23 functions carrying a
header-domain load inside a loop. Intel Xeon @ 2.80GHz, LLVM 18, --profile
speed, minimum of 7 alternating rounds, taskset -c 0
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: a generic may be exported and instantiated from another module
entries.body:
WP18 G7, the whole-program half of generics. A template declared in one module
can now be imported and instantiated anywhere: each (template, type-argument
tuple) is defined exactly once, in the module that declares the template, and
every other module emits a `declare` carrying that definition's attributes. One
imported name becomes one symbol per distinct tuple rather than one symbol,
which is the whole of what makes a template unlike every other import. The two
refusals that stood in for this milestone are deleted; their codes, NL2298 and
NL2316, are retired and reserved.

**The request crosses a module boundary; the work does not.** A template is
monomorphised in the scope it was declared in, because that is the only scope
its annotations and its body mean anything in, so `instantiate` forwards to the
declaring module and keeps only the *site*: the file the call was written in,
and the instantiation whose body made it. That is what a termination or cap
refusal is reported against, and it is what lets the termination rule's chain
follow a request across modules.

**It closes the trap §16 marked.** An instantiation's symbol was minted from the
*instantiating* module's package prefix, which was correct only while importing
a template was refused — the module that instantiated was always the module
that declared. It is the template's now, in `instantiate` and in
`collectInstanceMembers`, where the two `TODO(WP18 G7)` lines were. Without
that, two packages importing one generic mint one symbol for two different
functions and the whole-program fact table in `codegen/attributes.ts`, which is
keyed by symbol, hands one instantiation the other's purity and escape facts:
a miscompile rather than a link error.

**A type argument carries its layout across.** `identity<Point>` puts a
`%struct.Point` into a module that has never heard of `Point`, so the request
brings the layout and the answer brings back whatever the instantiated class
itself reaches — both through the closure an imported class already goes
through. A layout going *out* brings no symbols, because the language has no
way to call a member of a type parameter.

**A signature annotation could only write its request down.** Pass 1 resolves a
module's annotations as soon as it is parsed, which is what makes an import
cycle legal, so `Box<i32>` in an exported signature is read before any import is
bound. The name is knowable anyway, so the annotation resolves to the struct it
will be and the request is made in a sub-pass after every module has bound —
which is also where this milestone's one new rule lives: a type-argument list on
an imported name that is not a template (NL2325).

Measured: one `define` per instantiation over four modules, 5,144 B linked;
IR(stage0) == IR(stage1) byte for byte on every new case, bootstrap unmoved
Refs: docs/wp18-generics.md §15.5, docs/LANGUAGE.md
Tests: tests/link/generic_import, generic_two_importers, generic_import_chain,
package_generic_import, generic_import_private, generic_import_no_args,
generic_import_plain, tests/wordings/nl2325_type_args_on_import
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: decide the three proposed rows, and the questions they answer
entries.body:
WP23 §4 to §6 stood as proposals to be reviewed. Each already carried its own
argument to a recommendation; what was missing was the verdict, and a note whose
rows are all answered is worth more to the M4 freeze than one whose last three
are open. So the recommendations become decisions, the sections that argued them
are untouched, and each heading gains a paragraph saying what was decided and
what would turn it.

**§4, module-level mutable state — no.** One candidate, whose whole content is a
boolean a driver already parsed, against a new IR construct, the first writable
global the compiler defines for user code, a symbol in the flat namespace WP21
has to fix, and a thread-local decision taken years before WP20 lands. §4 stays
as the design. The revisit trigger is the count §4.6 proposed — two more places
in `self/` wanting it for a reason that is *not* a CLI flag — and §10 question 3,
which asked whether a count or a WP20 stage was the right trigger, is answered by
taking the count: a count is falsifiable by reading the corpus.

The divergence §4.6 names is **not** closed by this and is recorded as still
owed: `self/ice.ts`'s `internalError` prints the human report and not the
`NL0003` object stage0 prints, so orientation rule 7 is a stated contract stage1
does not honour. The comment beside it gives module state as one of its three
reasons, and that reason is now answered — the remedy is `json` on `Options` and
one parameter through the callers, and it needs no language change.

**§5, pairs and multiple return — yes, as a library type, and the gate is
already open.** §5.4 read the gate as "when WP18 is green" and it is narrower
than that: G5 gave a generic interface more than one type parameter and G7 made a
template exportable, which together are the whole of what a library type is. The
four lines §5.2 designed compile and link today, checked by compiling them rather
than asserted; G6 and G8 are not prerequisites. §10 question 5 — `std/` or each
program — is answered because its premise expired: there is a `std/` now.

**§6, compile-time function parameters — not scheduled.** §6.4's trigger is WP18
landed plus two real programs asking, and this records the first: wp29 §6 names
this row as the prerequisite for its P1 and nothing else on that page needs a
language feature that does not exist. wp29 §6 gains the other half of that
sentence, so its P1 reads as gated on a second ask rather than on an argument
nobody has had.

None of the three adds a rule to LANGUAGE.md, which takes all three off M4's
critical path — §11's first bullet said that was undecided and it is decided now.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: register the cases stage1's parser refuses, and fail when the set moves
entries.body:
WP19 §5's R3 row stated a caveat against its own declaration: the reject
oracle's parser bucket was a count in a summary line with nothing comparing it
to a ceiling, so the next rule to leave the parser's reach would migrate a case
into it silently. The row's own remedy — "read the bucket's number across such
a change" — is an instruction to a person, which is the same class of gate as a
number in a document: it holds until somebody forgets.

`tests/self/parser_refusals.txt` is the ceiling instead: 89 entries, each a case
and the sentence stage1 answers with, modelled on `tests/self/stage1_only.txt`
down to its header. The comparison fails in both directions, so the register
shrinks as rules move back into the checker's reach rather than only growing.

It also watches itself fail. `auditRegister` is a function of what a run
observed and nothing else, and `selfCheck` drives it over fabricated inputs
before a compiler is built — eight cases over the four failures and the four
silences that frame them, each watched failing under a separate mutation of the
audit. Without it a green run is one where all four branches are unreached, and
deleting any of them would have changed no assertion in `npm test`.
metrics: 8 self-check cases, 4 mutations of the audit watched failing, 0 of them visible to `npm test` before
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: --json carries a syntax error, and a column counts code units
entries.body:
`--json` is one of the two machine-readable contracts the compiler promises —
one flat object per diagnostic, every failure expressed as one of them — and
`VARIATIONS` in `tests/self/parity.js` had never named it. The cross product
that compares the two compilers on every surface a command line produces had
therefore never asked them the question a CI consumer asks.

Adding the variation found 180 undeclared differences over 901 programs, all of
them on `--json`, and 178 were one defect: `Compilation.load` wrote the
parser's refusals to stderr with `writeError` whatever the command line said,
so stage1 answered a syntax error with an empty stdout where stage0 printed an
object. The diagnostics go into the sink now, where stage0 has always put its
own, and the driver decides the stream.

Two spans were narrowed to the thing their message names — `__proto__` in
stage1, `debugger` in stage0 — and one class had **no rows at all**: a
diagnostic column counted bytes in stage1 where stage0 counts UTF-16 code
units, in the default mode, under no flag. It measured zero because no corpus
program put a non-ASCII character in front of a caret, and both
`self/diagnostics.ts` and `self/debug.ts` had written that caveat down and then
retired it on the strength of the ASCII goldens. `tests/cases/reject_diag_utf8`
is what makes the corpus ask from here on, and its `.err` pins the column so
`npm test` enforces the rule rather than only the nightly.

No miscompile: every `.ll` file was byte-identical between the two compilers
under every variation, before the fixes and after them.
metrics: 180 undeclared differences before, 0 after, over 14432 runs and 902 programs
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: exercise the aarch64 and darwin rows before a release attaches them
entries.body:
Three rows of `.github/seed-targets.json` carried `attachedSince: 0.4.0` and
none had ever run, while the 0.4.0 release pull request was open. That file's
own note says why that is not recoverable: `ci.yml`'s `bootstrap` matrix is
built from what a release *carries*, not from `attachedSince`, so the release
that first attaches a seed gives that platform a row on every push from then
on, and rolling the version back does not clear it.

All three were exercised first, on their own hardware, and all three pass. So
`0.4.0` is a promise those rows can keep — proved rather than assumed.

Getting there settled the Mach-O `stage3 == stage2` comparison, which had been
red as *unattributed* and blamed on a debug map that a `--profile speed` link
never emits. The differing bytes are `LC_UUID`'s, and the failure was the
harness's rather than the toolchain's: `bootstrap.sh` linked stage2 at
`$work/stage2` and stage3 at `$work/stage3`, so two compilers that agreed about
every other byte were guaranteed two different UUIDs. Both are linked at one
path now and moved into place afterwards. The comparison is still a raw `cmp`
of the two files — nothing relaxed, nothing masked, no load command dropped —
and it holds on Mach-O as it does on ELF.

`-Wl,-no_uuid` is closed off with evidence rather than left as a proposal: it
links, and then dyld on arm64 refuses the image, so the stage aborts before it
compiles anything.

What the UUID varies with is deliberately not claimed. Measured: it is stable
across two links to one output path and differs on a link to another, which
rules out a hash of the output's own content. Not established: whether it is
the path or something that had changed by the third link, because the probe
never returned to the first. The remedy does not rest on the answer.
metrics: three seed rows green through bootstrap --verify, the tarball check and the smoke test; both darwin rows byte-identical
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: cut the ddc provenance tag from the release that proves it
entries.body:
WP19 G6 asks for one tag — `ddc-<version>`, on the last commit at which
`IR(stage0, self/) == IR(stage1, self/)` and the fixed point both hold — and
writes down the four-step procedure for re-verifying the property from it. The
paragraph existed; the tag did not, and nothing in the repository would ever
have cut one. So G6 was a procedure for checking out a tag that does not exist,
and it would have stayed that way until the release where somebody happened to
remember — which is the release after the one where they did not.

It is the cheapest gate in the document and the only one that is unrecoverable:
after R6 deletes `src/` there is no second implementation left to disagree with,
so a release that forgets the tag is the release after which nothing can be said
about diverse double-compiling at all.

`.github/ddc-tag.sh` decides whether a release may carry the tag and what it is
named. It proves nothing itself and must not grow a proof — the property is
proved by `tests/self/bootstrap.js` inside `npm test` in the `ci` job, and by
`scripts/bootstrap.sh --verify` with stage0 as the seed on every `binaries` row
— and the script reads what those jobs answered through `DDC_PROOF`. A job that
did not run reports an empty result, and a `needs:` edited to drop one reports
nothing at all, which is the same answer: the proof did not run, and neither may
tag. `release.yml` gains a `ddc` job needing `[ci, targets, binaries]`, and
`release` now needs it, so the tag is cut after the proof and before the
publish — a release that then fails to publish leaves a tag naming a commit at
which the property did hold, and the re-run is green.

Every arm is driven from `tests/run.js` against a stand-in for git, and every
arm was also exercised end to end against real git in a throwaway bare
repository, because a stand-in can only be as right as its author's model of
git. That is how the first defect was found: `git ls-remote --tags origin
refs/tags/<tag>` never returns the peeled `refs/tags/<tag>^{}` line, so an
annotated tag's answer is its tag object's sha, which equals no commit — a tag
cut by hand on exactly the released commit read as a tag that had moved, and
with `release` needing this job that is a release nobody can cut. Both patterns
are asked for now, and a failed `ls-remote` is a refusal of its own rather than
being read as "no tag exists".

The version check was corrected in review to refuse what its comment claims: it
had accepted `123-fix-bug`, an ordinary issue-numbered branch, while claiming to
refuse "what is not a version at all". It is dotted integers with at most one
`-suffix` and one `+build` now, deliberately still a superset of what
`.github/seed-due.sh` accepts, so this can never refuse at the last step before
a publish a release that the one script deciding releasability allowed.
metrics: 19 checks over every arm of the script, 4 deliberate mutations watched failing
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: re-measure every gate and state what R6 is still waiting on
entries.body:
Every gate state in WP19 was true on the day it was written, and several had
stopped being true. They are replaced with measurements taken on merged `main`,
each carrying its date and the command that produced it, so M6's remaining
distance is a list rather than a recollection.

§5a is new and does the part the gate table cannot: it answers whether R6 is a
decision somebody makes or a project somebody schedules, by sorting what stands
between into three kinds — closed and measured, open work that needs an
afternoon, and a human's decision. A row in the wrong bucket is how "we are
nearly there" survives contact with a year, which is why they are separated
rather than listed as one backlog.

§A8 is new and records the `--json` result as the fifth way this gate has
reported green while something was wrong, and the one the previous four could
not have found: the cross product is only ever as wide as `VARIATIONS`. 180
undeclared differences on an otherwise-green corpus, 178 of them one defect
across 89 programs, and a fourth class with zero rows — a diagnostic column
counting bytes against UTF-16 code units, in the default mode under no flag,
invisible because no corpus program put a non-ASCII character in front of a
caret. §A5 gains the third instance of the pathology it catalogues: a caveat
written down in `self/diagnostics.ts` and then retired against ASCII goldens,
the same move `self/debug.ts` made.

What the gates now say: G1 green over the corpus on `862c7cc`, G2's wording
half green with the count and the tool, G3 and G5 closed by `acbca9f` with the
Mach-O `LC_UUID` difference traced to the harness linking stage2 and stage3 at
different paths — stated as the leading explanation rather than as a finding,
because the probe never returned to the first path and path-identity is
confounded with invocation order. G6 closed by `21a9381`, which merged during
this pull request's review; the check count is derived from the command rather
than copied from that description, which said 18 where the tree has 19.

G5 stays open on a decision rather than an oversight: the installer has no
registry name, `nish` on npm having belonged to somebody else since 2014.

And the section on being ready to delete says plainly that this week's evidence
points the other way. §7's trigger is a release cycle in which stage0 found
nothing; in the run that produced these numbers, stage0 caught a
machine-readable contract stage1 was not answering at all across 89 programs,
and each compiler caught a span the other got wrong. A document arguing for
retirement while its own measurements pointed away from it would be the exact
failure this package has now recorded five times.
metrics: 14432 runs over 902 programs, 0 undeclared differences, on 862c7cc
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: date every gate state, and correct four stale variation counts
entries.body:
The acceptance check against merged `main` found six gate states carrying a
merge SHA or a bare command where the rule asks for a date and the command that
produced it. Each is re-derived on `7ff7ce1` and dated here.

§3 G4 had no state paragraph at all, and gains one that deliberately does not
invent a command. That gate's claim is documentary rather than behavioural —
the policy sentence is in `wp12-release.md` under "The bootstrap seed" — so the
paragraph says what would falsify it instead: that heading going away, or a
release cut against a seed the sentence does not name. The rest of §3 carries a
command because those rows assert something about the tree's behaviour; this one
does not, and a dated run of something unrelated would be worse than none.

§3 G5, §5 R2 and §5 R4 gain the checks behind them — `node tests/run.js seed`
38 passed, `wp12` 57, `bootstrap` 12, 0 failed — and §3 G6 and §5 R5 gain the
date the ddc-tag count was taken on.

§5 R3 still read "344 of 408 codes provoked, 64 unreachable", accurate for
2026-09-18 and superseded twenty lines later by §5a's 344/410 and 66. Both are
present now with the command, and the row classifies the defect rather than
merely fixing it: not a claim that was wrong, which is what §A5 collects, but
one that stopped being current — an accurate record of one day sitting in a
table a reader takes for the tree's present state. The remedy is the same and
cheaper, re-derive rather than re-read, which is why both numbers name the
command.

Review caught the same shape once more. The sentence recording that #116's
description said 18 ddc-tag checks where the tree has 19 attributed that 19 to
`node tests/run.js ddc-tag`, which prints 31 — the filter also selects the
`verify-binaries:` checks. The number was right and its provenance was wrong,
one turn after that sentence was written to record a number whose provenance was
wrong. Both places now carry a command a reader can paste and say what the bare
filter answers instead.

Outside WP19, `VARIATIONS` has sixteen entries and four files said otherwise:
`.claude/testing.md` and `std/README.md` said fourteen, `docs/wp26-stdlib.md`
fourteen, `docs/wp10-ci.md` fifteen. Two of the four turned up by sweeping for
the phrase rather than by being reported. `.claude/testing.md` is a file agents
are told to read before writing code, so being two revisions behind there has a
cost.
metrics: coverage 344/410 codes, 66 unreachable; 19 ddc-tag checks; VARIATIONS 16
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: take @amritk/nish as the package name, and keep nish as the command
entries.body:
`nish` on the public registry has belonged to somebody else since 2014, and
`wp12-release.md` has carried the three ways out as an open decision ever since:
a scope, a different bare name, or npm's dispute process. The scope is taken.

`package.json#name` is `@amritk/nish`; `bin.nish` is untouched, so
`src/branding.ts` and `self/branding.ts` — the two files the whole compiler
reads its name from — do not move and no diagnostic changes a byte. That is
option (a) without the project rename option (b) would have carried, and it is
the option the note already argued for: (a) is reversible into the other two and
neither of them is reversible into it.

What it costs is written down rather than left to be discovered. `npm publish`
needs `--access public` every time, which the commented-out publish step in
`release.yml` already carries. The install line and the command line stop being
one string. And `npm pack` names the tarball `amritk-nish-<version>.tgz` —
measured, not assumed: `.github/seed-matrix.sh` and `.github/seed-due.sh` key on
the native `*.tar.gz` rows and never on the npm tarball, so the bootstrap matrix
is unaffected.

One check moved with the decision rather than being relaxed around it.
`tests/nish/cli.ts` took the expected tool name from `package.json#name` and
asserted it against `--version` and the usage text. Both went red, and both were
right to: the name it wanted is the tool the user types, which is `bin`'s key,
and that was the same string as `name` only by coincidence until now. It reads
`bin`'s key.

`STD_PREFIX` stays `nish/` and is now deliberately not a spelling of
`package.json#name`, which both branding files' comments claimed. No available
name could have kept that identity, since it needed the bare `nish`. It costs
nothing while the standard library is resolved by the compiler rather than by
npm, and `wp12-release.md` records what WP21 has to decide the day it is not.

WP19 moves the installer out of the human-decision bucket and into the work: the
gate never depended on which name, only on there being one.
metrics: node tests/run.js wp12 57 passed, seed 38, ddc-tag 31, bootstrap 12, cli 14, 0 failed
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: decide which compiler the package ships, and correct (b)'s stale cost
entries.body:
`wp12-release.md` carried "which compiler the package ships" as an open
decision with three rows: ship `self/` and build on the user's machine (a),
per-platform prebuilt binaries as `optionalDependencies` (b), or make the
self-hosted native binary the thing `bin.nish` runs (c). It is decided, and one
of the two things holding it open had quietly stopped being true.

Recorded: **(c) for which binary, (b) for delivery, (a) as the fallback**, dated
2026-09-19. `bin.nish` runs the native compiler; `dist/` stays as the bootstrap
seed and the differential oracle and stops being the thing a user runs; the
binary arrives as per-platform packages, and a platform with no binary falls
back to (a). The rows were never alternatives — (c) says which binary is `nish`,
(b) says how it arrives, (a) is what (b) does when it has nothing to hand over.

(b)'s recorded cost was "a release build matrix that does not exist.
`release.yml` runs one `ubuntu-latest` job and attaches one tarball", and that
was the reason (b) was ruled out. Neither half is true: `release.yml`'s
`binaries` job is `runs-on: ${{ matrix.target.runner }}` (line 165) over
`fromJSON(needs.targets.outputs.rows)` (line 171) with `fail-fast: false` (line
169) — one runner per target architecture, nothing cross-compiled — and the
`release` job attaches the npm tarball plus every asset the matrix produced.
`acbca9f` (#114) exercised the three rows `.github/seed-targets.json` marks
`attachedSince: 0.4.0` on the hardware each names, and all three passed. The
fourth, `x86_64-linux`, is `attachedSince: 0.1.1` and needed no exercising: the
job has built and attached it at every release since.

The correction names the mechanism rather than only the fact, because that is
what this neighbourhood of the document is about: nothing edited the cost into
being wrong. It was true when written, the matrix was then built for the seed
protocol's sake rather than for this decision, and the sentence went stale where
it stood while still reading like a measurement.

What honestly remains of (b)'s cost is stated instead: N+1 packages published
per release, and a fallback for a platform with no binary — which is (a), so the
two are additive rather than exclusive.

One dangling reference elsewhere in the file is fixed in passing, because
`check-links.mjs` cannot see it: the prose near the top pointed at a section
called "Open decision: the npm name is taken", which ec1b1c7 renamed to "The
npm name", and said the tarball install was needed "because the registry name
is not ours" — which stopped being true when `@amritk/nish` was taken. It now
says nothing is published yet, and why.

The options table is untouched, including (b)'s stale cell, because it is the
record of the reasoning and the stale cell is the example. The heading keeps its
"Open decision" wording so `wp19-stage0-retirement.md`'s inbound anchor still
resolves; the note says so, and renaming it is a change of its own.

Nothing is implemented. `package.json` still ships `dist/`, `files` still does
not list `self/`, no per-platform package exists, and the G5 installer has not
been designed. Documentation only.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: a section that records a decision should not be headed "Open decision"
entries.body:
`cba05b0` recorded which compiler the package ships and left the heading
saying the opposite, because renaming it meant repointing a link in
`wp19-stage0-retirement.md` while that file had work in flight. It does
not any more, so the rename and the link land together here.

Four sentences went stale with the two decisions of 2026-09-19 and are
corrected with it:

- wp19 §5a still said the installer "waits on one more decision of its
  own, which compiler the package ships". That decision was answered by
  `cba05b0`, so nothing in that item waits on a person now.
- The "Not in this work package" bullet said the 0.4.0 rows "wait on a
  run that exercises their rows, the darwin pair additionally on the
  ld64 fixed point". `acbca9f` ran all three on their own hardware and
  settled the Mach-O comparison; what they wait on is a release.
- The same bullet said delivering through npm "waits on the name". The
  name landed in `ec1b1c7`.
- Release step 4 said publishing is "blocked on the name". It is blocked
  on the installer, and `--access public` stopped being conditional on
  which name wins the moment a scoped one did.

Three of those were bare prose in quotation marks rather than Markdown
links -- `see "Open decision: ..."` -- which is why `check-links.mjs` was
green across both renames and why one of them had been wrong since
`ec1b1c7`. A quoted heading title is a reference the link checker cannot
see, and this is the second rename in two days to leave one behind.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: install the compiler from npm or from curl, as a prebuilt binary
entries.body:
There are two ways to install the compiler now, and both are a download
rather than a build: `npm install -g @amritk/nish`, and a `curl | sh` of
`install.sh`. **Nothing is compiled on a user's machine on any path.**

`bin.nish` becomes a launcher, because npm cannot point a `bin` entry at a
dependency that may or may not be installed. The native compiler arrives as
one `@amritk/nish-<asset>` package per row of `.github/seed-targets.json`,
declared as an `optionalDependencies` entry with `os` and `cpu` set, so npm
fetches the one that matches and skips the rest. A platform with no prebuilt
binary runs `dist/index.js`, the Node compiler already in the package.

Neither channel needed new build machinery. `release.yml`'s `binaries` job
already staged what both want -- `bin/nish` beside the `runtime/` and
`scripts/` it resolves one level up from itself -- so the platform package is
`npm pack` over that directory, and the script downloads the tarball that job
has attached since 0.1.1.

This amends a decision rather than overwriting it. The fallback for a platform
with no binary was recorded as (a), shipping `self/` and bootstrapping; that
costs a clang and two compilations of `self/` on the user's machine plus
944,676 bytes in every tarball on every platform, to serve musl and FreeBSD.
"`dist/` stops being the thing a user runs" and "never, on any platform, even
when there is no binary" are two claims, and only the first was argued.

The work measured a defect the retirement note recorded as unmeasured:
`packageRoot()`'s sensitivity to `argv[0]` (wp19 §5a item 4). A bare `nish` on
`$PATH` arrives with no directory in `argv[0]`, so the compiler resolves
`./..` and every `--link` fails against the working directory -- while
`--version` and `-o` keep working, which is why nothing had noticed.
Unpacking a release tarball onto `$PATH` was therefore not an install. Both
installers work around it with a one-line `exec` of an absolute path; the
defect itself stays open, because the fix belongs in `self/`.
metrics: 3.2 ms per invocation after the postinstall swap, against 94 ms through the node launcher and 2.7 ms for the binary run directly
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: an apostrophe in a comment truncated the release train's version bump
entries.body:
`release-pr.yml` runs its version bump as `node -e '...'`, and #124 added a
comment to that script reading `release's binaries`. The apostrophe closed the
shell string, so node was handed a truncated program and the step died with
`SyntaxError: Unexpected end of input`.

The YAML was valid, the JavaScript was valid, and the shell quoting was not,
which is why nothing caught it. It broke on the merge that introduced it
(`c2c76da`), after changelog-gen had already written changelog/0.4.0.json --
so `Open or refresh the Release pull request` was skipped and no 0.4.0 release
pull request exists. Nothing partial landed on main; the runner threw its
working copy away.

The real defect is that nothing ran the step. It is a workflow step, so it
executes once per merge to main, in the one place where a failure stops the
release train instead of a pull request, and the person who finds out is
whoever next wanted to cut a release. So `tests/run.js` now extracts the
`node -e` block from the workflow and RUNS it against copies of package.json,
package-lock.json and self/branding.ts, asserting all four things it is
supposed to move: the version, both of the lockfile's copies of it, every
platform package pinned in optionalDependencies, and VERSION in
self/branding.ts.

Extracted rather than restated, for the reason `.github/seed-matrix.sh` and
`.github/seed-due.sh` are run rather than read: a second copy of the bump
would agree with the first until one of them was edited, which is the failure
this guard is for. Re-introducing the apostrophe turns the new check red,
which is how it was checked.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon
